In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah al-Hajj

Ibn ʿAbbas said, according to the more apparent of the two reports: it is Meccan, except for the words of God Most High, ﴿These two adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord﴾, and two verses after this verse, and His words, Most High, ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged...﴾, the verse. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas in another report that this surah is Madinan, except for some verses which were revealed in Mecca.

His words, Most High, ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾: that is, beware of His punishment by obeying Him. It is also said: "Fear your Lord" means: avoid all the prohibited things, among which is polytheism and other things.

His words: ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour﴾. Zalzalah (convulsion) is an intense movement in a terrifying state. Opinions differ regarding this convulsion. ʿAlqamah and al-Shaʿbi mention that it is before the Day of Resurrection, while Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi and others mention that it occurs at the establishment of the Hour. This second opinion is the more correct of the two, due to the report we will mention below.

His words: ﴿is a tremendous thing﴾: that is, a great matter.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿The Day you see it﴾ means: the Hour.

And His saying: ﴿will distract﴾ means: will make one heedless and preoccupied. It also means: will make one forgetful and oblivious. A poet said about *dhuhul* (distraction):

(Days have lengthened with you until you forgot her,
as if you were distracted from the Day of Resurrection.)

ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawaha said in the presence of the Prophet:

(A striking that removes the skull from its resting place,
and makes the close friend forget his close friend.)

And His saying: ﴿every nursing mother will forget what she nursed﴾ means: every mother will forget her child.

And His saying: ﴿and every pregnant woman will drop her burden﴾. If someone asks: How can a woman drop her burden on the Day of Resurrection? The answer: As for our view that the quaking occurs before the Hour arrives, then the meaning of dropping the burden is literal. If we say that the quaking occurs at the Hour's arrival, then the answer has two aspects. The first: the verse refers to women who die while pregnant. The second aspect, which is the more correct: this is an expression of the magnitude of the matter and the mention of the intensity of the terror, not the literal dropping of a burden. The Arabs say: "A matter befell us in which the youth turns grey," and this is in the manner of emphasizing the greatness and severity of the matter. God Almighty also said: ﴿a Day that will turn children grey-haired﴾, and what is meant is what we have explained.

And His saying: ﴿and you will see people as intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated﴾. It is also read *sukra* without the alif, and the meaning is the same. What the people of exegesis (*ahl al-tafsir*, the scholars of Qur'anic interpretation) hold is that the verse means: intoxicated from terror and fear, and they are not intoxicated from wine. They also said: "in the form of the intoxicated, yet they are not intoxicated." The first view is better, because God Almighty said: ﴿but the punishment of God is severe﴾.

In the verse there is a sound report which al-Bukhari and others transmitted, namely what al-A'mash related from Abu Salih, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that the Prophet recited it between the two verses, then said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, God Almighty will say to Adam: Stand up, O Adam, and send forth from your offspring the group for the Fire. Adam will say: At Your service, and at Your pleasure, and the good is in Your hands. And what is the group for the Fire? God Almighty will say: From every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire, [and one] to Paradise. The Companions of the Messenger of God said: And which of us is that one? The Prophet said: Be steadfast, draw near, and rejoice, for with you are two peoples who have never been with a group except that they outnumbered it: Gog and Magog, and the disbelievers of the jinn and mankind from among those before you."

In another narration he said: "Nine hundred and ninety-nine from Gog and Magog, and one from among you." Then he said: "I truly hope that you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise," so we exclaimed "Allahu akbar." Then he said: "I truly hope that you will be a third of the people of Paradise," so we exclaimed "Allahu akbar." Then he said: "I truly hope that you will be half of the people of Paradise. You are not, on that Day, among the people except like a white hair on a black ox, or like a black hair on a white ox."

In another narration: "You are not among the people except like a mole on the flank of a camel, or like a spot on the foreleg of a beast."

The Shaykh, the Imam said: Al-Makki ibn ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us of this hadith, saying: My grandfather Abu al-Haytham informed us, saying: al-Firabri said, al-Bukhari said: ʿUmar ibn Hafs ibn Ghiyath said: My father informed us, from al-A'mash… the report.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 3:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge﴾. Most of the scholars hold that the verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to deny the Resurrection and dispute about it. On the authority of Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah, regarding this verse, he said: it refers to one who disputes about the signs of Allah according to his own desires. On the authority of another, he said: it refers to one who rejects the explicit text by means of analogy (qiyas).

As for His saying: ﴿and follows every devil, rebellious﴾. The marid (rebellious) is the one who is defiant, and the one who is defiant is the one who persists in evil. It is said: "a wall that is mumarrad," meaning: lengthened (or extended). It is also said: the marid is the one who is bare of good, as it is said: "a boy amrad," when his cheeks are bare of hair.

"And His words, ﴿It was decreed concerning him﴾, meaning: concerning the Shaytan.

And His words, ﴿that whoever takes him as a friend, he will certainly lead him astray﴾, meaning: it was decreed for the Shaytan that he would lead astray whoever takes him as a friend.

And His words, ﴿and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾, meaning: to the punishment of Jahannam."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 5:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection﴾. In this verse Allah mentions the proof against those who deny the Resurrection, and the address is to the polytheists.

And His words: ﴿if you are in doubt about the Resurrection﴾, meaning: if you are in doubt about the Resurrection.

And His words: ﴿Indeed, We created you from dust﴾. Dust is mentioned here because Adam was created from dust, and it is the origin.

And His words: ﴿then from a sperm-drop﴾. The nutfah (sperm-drop) is the water that issues from the loins.

And His words: ﴿then from a clinging clot﴾. The 'alaqah (clinging clot) is congealed blood, and it is said: coagulated blood.

And His words: ﴿then from a lump of flesh﴾. The mudghah (lump of flesh) is a piece of flesh as if it had been chewed.

And His words: ﴿formed and unformed﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿formed﴾ means fully formed, and ﴿unformed﴾ means incompletely formed. The second view is that the formed is the child that the woman brings forth at its due time, and the unformed is the miscarriage. On this point there are reports. Among them is what 'Alqamah reported from Ibn Mas'ud, that when the sperm-drop settles in the womb, the angel takes it in his hand and says: "O Lord, formed or unformed?" If He says: "Unformed," the womb expels it as blood, and no living soul is formed from it. If He says: "Formed," the angel says: "Wretched or happy? Male or female? What is its provision? What is its deed? What is its term? And where is the place where it will die?" Then Allah the Exalted says to him: "Go to the Mother of the Book, for in it is all of that." So he goes to the Mother of the Book and finds in it that he is wretched or happy, male or female, and he writes that down. Then the man strives in his deed, eats his provision, and proceeds through his term until Allah the Exalted takes his soul in the place He has decreed.

Two sound reports have also come from the Prophet on this. One is what al-A'mash reported from Zayd ibn Wahb from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Truthful and Believed One, Abu al-Qasim, informed me: "Indeed the creation of each of you is gathered in his mother's womb for forty days as a sperm-drop, then forty days as a clot, [then Allah says: "that We may make clear to you"], then forty days as a lump of flesh. Then the angel is commanded with four words: he writes down his provision, his deed, his term, and whether he is wretched or happy. Then the spirit is breathed into him." This report is agreed upon as sound.

The second report is what Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah reported from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: I heard 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud say: "The wretched is one who is wretched in his mother's belly, and the happy is one who is admonished by others." Abu al-Tufayl said: I said: "May you be bereft of me! Shall we be wretched while we have not acted?" So I went to Hudhayfah ibn Usayd and mentioned to him the saying of Ibn Mas'ud. He said: "Shall I not inform you of something more wondrous than this? I heard the Messenger of Allah say: 'When the sperm-drop remains in the mother's womb forty days, or forty-five, the angel comes and says: O Lord, male or female? And the Lord decrees, and the angel writes. Then he says: Wretched or happy? And the Lord decrees, and the angel writes. Then he says: What is its provision, what is its deed, what is its term, what is its trace, what is its misfortune? Then Allah decrees what He wills, and the angel writes. Then he folds the scroll, and nothing is added to it or subtracted from it until the Day of Resurrection.'" The Shaykh, the Imam, said: This hadith was related to us by Abu 'Ali al-Shafi'i in Mecca, may Allah protect it, who said: Abu al-Hasan ibn [Faras] said: Abu Ja'far al-Dayboli related to us, who said: Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi said: Sufyan said... the report. It is recorded by Muslim in his Sahih.

And they recited poetry about the formed:

(Is it over the unformed that there is weeping? Then where is resolve, woe to you, and modesty?)

And His words: ﴿that We may make clear to you﴾, meaning: that We may make clear to you the matter of creation at its beginning, so that you may draw evidence (from the power of Allah shown in: ﴿And We cause whom We will to remain in the wombs for an appointed term, then We bring you out as infants, then that you may reach your maturity. And among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known﴾) at the beginning, of His power to bring back.

And His words: ﴿And We cause whom We will to remain in the wombs﴾, meaning: We establish in the wombs whom We will. ﴿for an appointed term﴾, meaning: until the time of birth.

And His words: ﴿then We bring you out as infants﴾, meaning: as children; it is singular used in the sense of plural.

And His words: ﴿then that you may reach your maturity﴾. We have already explained the meaning of ashudd (maturity).

And His words: ﴿And among you is one who is taken in death﴾. Abu Hatim related that in the reading of some, it was recited: "wa-minkum man yatawaffa" with a fatha on the ya', meaning: his term is fully completed. The well-known reading is ﴿yutawaffa﴾ with a damma, meaning: he is taken before reaching old age.

And His words: ﴿and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾, meaning: to the most base age. What is intended is the state of senility and decrepitude. 'Ikrimah said: whoever recites the Qur'an will not become senile.

And His words: ﴿so that he knows nothing after having known﴾, meaning: he does not understand anything, with his intellect having been lost.

And His words: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless﴾. This is mention of another proof of the revival of the dead.

And His words: ﴿lifeless﴾, meaning: dry and barren, with no vegetation in it. Qatadah said: (lifeless) means dusty and crumbled. It is also said: lifeless means effaced. The poet said:

(Qutayla said: "What ails your body, pale, and I see your garments worn and lifeless?")

Another said:

(Calamity of the times struck the women of the family of Harb, with a visitation that left them lifeless, having left them lifeless.)

(It turned their black hair white, and turned their white faces black.)

And His words: ﴿Then when We send down water upon it, it stirs﴾, meaning: it moves. The poet said:

(She sways when she stands, and quivers when she walks, as the branch of the ban-tree quivers in green foliage.)

And His words: ﴿and swells﴾, meaning: it swells for vegetation. It is also said: there is inversion in the verse, and its meaning is: it swells and stirs. It is said it stirs, meaning the vegetation, and swells, meaning rises. It is feminine only because of the feminine noun "earth." Abu Ja'far recited "wa-rabat" with hamza, which has the same meaning as the first.

And His words: ﴿and it grows from every lovely pair﴾, meaning: a fine kind. This too is a proof of the re-creation of creatures. And among what is transmitted from the early pious: "When you see the spring, remember the resurrection."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 6:

And His saying: ﴿That is because Allah, He is the Truth﴾ means: this which I have mentioned to you is [evidence] that Allah, He is the Truth.

And His saying: ﴿and that He gives life to the dead﴾ means: it is evidence that He gives life to the dead.

And His saying: ﴿and that He is Able over all things﴾ means: since He is able to originate creation and to revive the dead earth, know that He is Able over all things.

And in some reports from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever comes on the Day of Resurrection with three [qualities], nothing will turn his face away from Paradise: one who knows that Allah alone has no partner, that the Hour is coming with no doubt about it, and that Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves."
And His saying: ﴿and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will raise up those who are in the graves﴾. We have already explained it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 22, verse 8:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge or guidance﴾, meaning: "and not any proof (hujjah)."

And His saying: ﴿nor a book giving light﴾, meaning: "nor a book that has light."

It is related in some reports that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, upon falsehood there is darkness, and indeed upon truth there is light."

And from some of them it is related that he said: "The possessor of falsehood is never honored, even if the moon rises from his pocket; and the possessor of truth is never humbled, even if the whole world rallies against him."

Know that the verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kaladah, and his disputing by denying the Resurrection and his striking of examples for that.

And His saying: ﴿turning aside his side﴾, meaning: twisting his neck. Ibn Jurayj said: he turns away from the truth out of arrogance.

And His saying: ﴿to lead astray from the way of God﴾, meaning: to lead people astray from the religion of God.

And His saying: ﴿for him in this world is disgrace﴾, meaning: humiliation. Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith was killed on the Day of Badr by ṣabr (execution of a bound captive), and no one was killed by ṣabr besides him and 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt.

And His saying: ﴿and We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the Burning﴾, meaning: the burning Fire.
"And His saying: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ — the verse — its meaning is apparent."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 11:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge﴾. Mujahid said: "On doubt." Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, grammarian and exegete) said: "On an edge" means: the way in religion, he does not enter into it as one firmly established, nor does he enter it wholeheartedly. It is also said: "And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge" means: on weakness, like one standing on the edge of a thing whose foot is weak and unsettled. Some said: "On an edge" means: on a condition (jiha), then he explained the condition, saying: ﴿If good befalls him, he is reassured by it﴾, meaning he remains steadfast in faith, is content with it, and is at rest in it.

His saying: ﴿And if a trial afflicts him﴾, meaning a test and a calamity.

His saying: ﴿he turns back on his face﴾, meaning he returns on his heels and apostatizes.

His saying: ﴿He has lost both this world and the Hereafter﴾. The loss in this world is the failure to attain what he hoped for and sought, and the loss in the Hereafter is abiding forever in the Fire. It is also said: the loss in this world is being killed in disbelief, and the loss in the Hereafter is what we have explained. Mujahid recited: "Khasir al-dunya wa al-akhira" (as a singular active participle).

His saying: ﴿That is the manifest loss﴾, meaning the clear loss.

The people of tafsir said: the verse was revealed concerning a group of polytheists, one of whom would believe; if his wealth increased, his body was healthy, and his mare foaled, he would say: "This is a good religion, and I have gained good from it," and he would be at rest in it. But if illness befell him, or his child died, or his wealth decreased, he would say: "Nothing but evil has befallen me from this religion," and he would turn back.

In some reports: "A man from the Jews embraced Islam, then his sight was lost, his wealth perished, and his child died. He came to the Prophet and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, release me from it (aqilni).' He said: 'Indeed Islam is not revoked.' He said: 'Since I entered this religion I have encountered nothing but evil; such and such has befallen me.' The Prophet said: 'Indeed Islam purifies a man as fire purifies the dross of gold, silver and iron.'" The report is gharib (weak/rare in transmission).

Al-Sam'ani's commentary on Surah 22, verse 12:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He calls upon, besides Allah, that which neither harms him nor benefits him﴾ meaning: it does not harm him if he does not worship it, and it does not benefit him if he worships it.

And the words of the Exalted: ﴿That is the far-off error﴾ meaning: the error that persists.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 13:

God's words: ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is closer than his benefit﴾. This verse is among the difficult passages of the Qur'an, and it raises questions. The first question: they said that in the first verse it says ﴿what does not harm him﴾, and here it says ﴿one whose harm﴾.

(How then is the reconciliation between them? The answer: the meaning of His words ﴿He calls upon one whose harm﴾ is:)

That is, one whose worship causes him harm. And His words in the first verse ﴿what does not harm him﴾ mean: it does not harm (him) if he abandons its worship, as we have explained.

The second question: they said that He says in this verse ﴿closer than his benefit﴾. The answer: this is according to the custom of the Arabs, who use such an expression while meaning that there is no benefit at all. This is like God's words ﴿That is a far-off return﴾, that is, no return at all.

The third question, which is the difficult one, is that He says ﴿one whose harm﴾. What is this construction? The answer: the grammarians differed on this. Most grammarians held that it is by inversion (taqdim and ta'khir), and its meaning is: he calls upon the one whose harm is closer than his benefit. As for al-Mubarrad, he rejected this and said: this is not permissible in the language. The answer to the question on this view: some said the meaning of ﴿calls upon﴾ (yad'u) is "says" (yaqul).

The poet said:

(They call out [Antarah] (while the swords) are like ... ropes of a well on the chest of the dark stallion)

That is, they say. On this reading the meaning of the verse is: he says, that is, he says of the one whose harm is closer than his benefit: "He is a god or a master." Others said: "he calls upon one whose harm..." means: to the one whose harm is closer than his benefit. Others said its meaning is: that is the far-off error, he calls upon, that is, during his calling; then he resumed and said: ﴿one whose harm is closer than his benefit. Wretched is the master, and wretched is the companion﴾. Others said: that is the far-off error, he calls upon, meaning: the one who is the far-off error calls upon; this has the sense of "the one who" (alladhi), and then he resumed his words: ﴿one whose harm is closer than his benefit﴾. This was chosen by al-Zajjaj. Ibn Faris, when relating most of these opinions, said: "Refer the verse to the one who knows it."

His words ﴿Wretched is the master﴾ mean: the helper. It was also said: the one worshipped.

His words ﴿and wretched is the companion﴾ mean: the associate and the close companion. The Arabs call a spouse "ashir" (companion) because of the close association.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed you (women) curse much and are ungrateful to the ashir," that is, the husband.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ and so on to the end of the verse; its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 15:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him⦆. Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah will not help Muhammad (ﷺ).

It is also narrated from him that he said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited Asad and Ghatafan to Islam, and there was an alliance between them and the People of the Book, they said: "We cannot embrace Islam and break the alliance, because Muhammad may not prevail and may not be victorious; then the alliance between us and the People of the Book would be severed, and they would not provide us with supplies." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

The second opinion: ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him⦆, that is, will not provide for him (yarzuqahu Allah). This applies to one who has a bad opinion of his Lord and fears that He will not provide for him.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the Arabs say "ard manswurah" (a land that is ﻿manṣūrah), meaning "mamtūrah" (rained upon). It is also reported from some Bedouins that he asked and said: "Unsurni yansurka Allah" (give me, and Allah will give you), meaning: "a'tini a'taka Allah" (give me, and may Allah give you).

As for His words: ﴿in this world and the Hereafter⦆, its meaning is clear.

As for His words: ﴿Let him stretch a rope to the sky⦆, the intended "sky" is the sky of his house according to all the exegetes, and it is the ceiling.

The word "sabab" means a rope; its meaning is: let him stretch a rope from the ceiling of his house. ﴿Then let him cut it off⦆, that is, let him strangle himself with it.

As for His words: ﴿Then let him see whether his scheme removes that which enrages him⦆, that is: does he have any means to deal with what enrages him, so as to repel it from himself? It is also said: then let him consider whether what he has done benefits him.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: this is like the saying of one who says: "If you are not pleased with such-and-such, then die of rage."
Al-Sam'ani, on God's words: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as clear signs﴾ ... the verse. Its apparent meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 17:

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate others with Allah﴾ — we have already explained this in Surat al-Baqarah.

And His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. If it is said: what is the meaning of repeating "inna" (indeed) at the end of the verse, when it was already mentioned at the beginning of the verse? The answer: the Arabs use this kind of repetition for emphasis. The poet said:

(Indeed the caliph, indeed Allah has clothed him / with the garment of kingship, by which the ends are hoped for)

And His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is a witness over everything﴾ — meaning: a Witness (shahid).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 18:

Regarding His words, ﴿Do you not see that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾, the verse, al-Zajjaj said: Prostration (sujud) here means obedience (ta'a), i.e., it obeys Him. They approved of this statement because it agrees with the Book, which is His words, ﴿Come willingly or unwillingly. They said, "We have come willingly."﴾ Also, the belief of the People of the Sunnah is that every animate and inanimate thing is wholly obedient to Allah, the Exalted. Some of them said: The prostration of stones is through the manifestation of the trace of creation in them, in the sense that one who contemplates and reflects upon them is led to prostration and humility. This is a corrupt view. The correct view is what we have mentioned before, and the evidence for it is that Allah, the Exalted, described stones with fear (khashyah), saying, ﴿And indeed among them is that which falls down out of fear of Allah﴾. It is not sound to interpret fear as the manifestation of the trace of power in them. Also, Allah, the Exalted, said, ﴿O mountains, echo back with him﴾, meaning: glorify with him. Had the intended meaning been the manifestation of the trace of creation, His words ﴿with David﴾ would have had no meaning, because David and others are equal in seeing the trace of creation. Also, Allah, the Exalted, said, ﴿And there is not a thing but exalts [Allah] by His praise﴾, meaning: obeys Allah by His glorification, ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾. Had the intended meaning of glorification been the manifestation of the trace of creation in it, His words ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾ would not be consistent. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, Ibrahim ibn al-Sari, mentioned these proofs, and Ibn Faris praised him, saying: He defended the religion and supported the Sunnah.

As for His words, ﴿and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the animals﴾, meaning: these things (all of them glorify Allah, the Exalted).

As for His words, ﴿and many of the people﴾, meaning: the Muslims.

As for His words, ﴿and many have deserved punishment﴾, they are the disbelievers, and the punishment is deserved for them here by their abandoning prostration. The meaning of the verse: and many of the people prostrate, so for them the punishment is deserved, [while those who refuse to prostrate are deserving of punishment].

As for His words, ﴿And whoever Allah humiliates, for him there is no bestower of honor﴾, meaning: whoever Allah makes wretched, for him there is no one who makes him happy. Some of them said: "whoever Allah humiliates" means whoever Allah abases, so for him there is no honoring, i.e., no one honors him.

﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them, poured over their heads with boiling water.﴾

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾, meaning: He honors and humiliates, and makes wretched and makes happy, by His will and His determination, and this is the belief of the People of the Sunnah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 19:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾. Regarding this verse there are several opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning the People of the Book and the Muslims. The People of the Book said: "Our religion is better than your religion, and we have a greater claim to Allah than you, because our Prophet and our Book are older." The Muslims said: "We have a greater claim to Allah than you, and our religion is better than your religion, because our Book overrides the (previous) books, and because our Prophet is the Seal of the Prophets." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. This is the view of Qatadah and a group of scholars.

The second: what is narrated from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: The verse was revealed concerning those who fought each other on the Day of Badr, from among the Muslims and the polytheists. The Muslims were: Hamzah, 'Ali, and 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith; and the polytheists were: Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah. So the verse was revealed concerning these six. Abu Dhar used to swear by Allah that the verse was revealed concerning these people. al-Bukhari mentioned it in the Sahih.

The third opinion: the verse was revealed concerning the whole body of Muslims and polytheists.

The fourth opinion: it was revealed concerning Paradise and Hellfire, which disputed with each other. Paradise said: "Allah created me so that He might show mercy through me," and Hellfire said: "Allah created me so that He might take vengeance through me." This is the view of 'Ikrimah. The well-known opinions are the first two. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah the Exalted mentioned six categories in His words: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and those who are Jews﴾, and so on, and He made five of them in the Fire and one for Paradise. Thus His words ﴿These two adversaries﴾ refer to them: the believers are one adversary, and the remaining five are the other adversary.

His words ﴿dispute concerning their Lord﴾ mean: they argued concerning their Lord.

His words ﴿So for those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them﴾ mean: molten brass. It is said that the Fire by which they are punished is called a garment because it encompasses them as a garment encompasses the body. Some have said: the people of the Fire will wear cut pieces of fire. This is the best of the opinions.

His words ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads﴾: this is water whose heat has reached its extreme. It is mentioned in the exegesis that if a single drop of it were placed upon the mountains of the world, it would melt them.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 20:

And His saying: ﴿Whereby there shall be melted﴾, i.e., melted by it. In the reports it is said that it pierces the head of the disbeliever and pours the boiling water (al-hamim) upon his skull, so that it reaches his interior and melts everything within his interior.

And His saying: ﴿and the skins﴾, i.e., it melts the skins and cooks them.

"And His saying: ﴿And for them are maqami' of iron﴾. The muqam'ah (maqma'ah) is the mirzabah of iron (a heavy iron club or mace). It is also said: it is the hirz of iron (an iron rod or bar). And it has been said: if one of them (a single muqam'ah of it) were placed in this world, and humankind and the jinn gathered together to lift it, they would not be able to lift it."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 22:

And His saying: ﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it, from distress﴾, i.e., they are driven back into it. It is said in the tafsir: the Fire surges with them and lifts them up to its top, so they wish to get out, but the zabaniyya (the angels of punishment) strike them with maqami' of iron (iron maces), and they plunge down into it for seventy autumns.

And His saying: ﴿And taste the punishment of the burning﴾, i.e., the angels say to them: taste the punishment of the burning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 23:

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who have believed and done righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ — its meaning is apparent.

And His saying: ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ — al-asawir (bracelets) is the plural of al-siwar (a bracelet).

And His saying: ﴿of gold﴾ — its meaning is known.

And His saying: ﴿and pearls﴾ — meaning: and of pearls.

It has also been recited as "lu'lu'an" (pearls, in the accusative), meaning: they will be adorned with pearls.

And His saying: ﴿and their clothing therein will be silk﴾ — meaning: of brocade (dibaj). Shu'bah narrated from Khalifah ibn Ka'b, from Ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "I heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter, and whoever does not wear it in the Hereafter will not enter Paradise, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and their clothing therein will be silk﴾.'"

And in some reports: "Even if he enters Paradise, he will not wear it in Paradise."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 24:

And His saying: ﴿And they were guided to good speech﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It is also said that it is: "Subhan Allah (Glory be to Allah), al-hamdu lillah (praise be to Allah), la ilaha illa Allah (there is no god but Allah), and Allah is greater (Allahu akbar)." It was also said: it is the saying of the people of Paradise: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾. And from Qutrub: that it is the Qur'an. It is also said: it is enjoining what is good (al-amr bi'l-ma'ruf). And it was said: it is the speech by which creation is praised and by which the Creator rewards.

And His saying: ﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾. That is, the path of Allah, and the path of Allah is Islam. It is also said: it refers to the lofty abodes.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 25:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾ (the sense of the verse is: indeed, the disbelievers and those who bar [others] from the way of Allah, and some of them said its meaning is: indeed, those who disbelieved previously and who bar [others] from the way of Allah) in the present.

And His saying: ﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning: they bar [others] from the Sacred Mosque.

And His saying: ﴿which We made for the people﴾, meaning: We made it for the people a qiblah for their prayers and a place of rites (manasik) for their Hajj.

And His saying: ﴿equal for the one who resides therein and the visitor﴾. It has been recited as "sawa'an al-'akif fihi wal-bad" with a fatha and tanwin. So His saying ﴿sawa'[un]﴾ with a damma is clear in meaning, while ﴿sawa'an﴾ with a fatha means: We made them equal (sawwaytahum sawa'an). And His saying ﴿al-'akif fihi wal-bad﴾ means: the one who resides in it, and the one who comes (to it).

They differ as to whether what is meant here is the entire Haram or the Sacred Mosque itself. One of the two views is that what is meant is the Sacred Mosque, and this is the view of al-Hasan and a group. The meaning of equality is equality in the honour of the Ka'bah and its excellence, and the excellence of circumambulation (tawaf) and all other acts of worship and their reward. The second view is that what is meant by the verse is the entire Haram, and the meaning of equality is that the resident of Makkah and the one who comes from Makkah are equal in alighting: whoever finds an empty place may alight, provided he does not disturb anyone. This is the view of Mujahid, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, 'Ata' and a group of the Tabi'un. 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) used to forbid people from locking their doors during the season (of Hajj). In another report, he prevented them from making doors, so a man made a door and he struck it with a whip (durra). In a report: the houses of Makkah used to be called "al-sawaib" (the free); whoever wished would reside, and whoever was free would lodge. According to this view, it is not permissible to sell or rent the houses of Makkah; according to the first view, it is permissible.

And His saying: ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation [in] wrongdoing﴾ (there are two views concerning it. One: the "ba'" is superfluous, and its meaning is: whoever intends therein deviation in wrongdoing). The poet said:

([We are the Banu Ja'dah, the people of al-Falaj... we strike with the sword and hope for relief])

﴿And [recall] when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House, [saying], "Do not associate anything with Me and purify My House for those who circumambulate and those who stand [in prayer]."﴾

That is: "tad'u al-farah" (you call for joy). This is the view of al-Farra' and the grammarians of Kufa. As for al-Mubarrad, he denied that the "ba'" is superfluous and said the meaning of the verse is: whoever has his intention therein to deviate with wrongdoing. The poet said:

(I wish to forget her, but it is as though Layla appears to me on every path)

Its meaning is: he intended to forget.

And His saying: ﴿We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾, meaning: a painful punishment will reach him. As for deviation (ilhad), it is inclination (al-mayl). It is said: "lahada" and "alhada" with the same meaning. Some said: "alhada" when one disputes, and "lahada" when one turns away from the truth. As for the meaning of ilhad here, some said: it is shirk. Some said: it is every evil, even a man cursing his slave. 'Ata' said: deviation in the Haram is that one enters without being in ihram, or commits a prohibited act of the Haram by killing game or uprooting a tree. If someone says: what is the meaning of specifying the Haram with all of this, when whoever commits an evil outside the Haram also deserves punishment? The answer: it is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: whoever intends a sin outside the Haram, it is not recorded against him; whoever intends a sin inside the Haram, it is recorded against him. And from him that he said: even if it is at Aden Abyan. Its meaning: even if he is far from the Haram, when he intends a sin within the Haram he is held accountable for it. This is the meaning of the "intention" mentioned in the verse.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And [remember] when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾, meaning: We made it clear to him and informed him. He mentioned "the place of the House" because the Ka'bah was raised up to the heaven at the time of the Flood. Then, when God, may He be exalted, commanded Abraham to build the House, He sent a strong wind (rīḥan khajjājā), which swept the site of the House until it revealed the place of the foundation. In another report: God sent a cloud the size of the House, in which there was a head that spoke, saying: "O Abraham, build according to my measure." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And [remember] when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾.

His saying: ﴿That you associate nothing with Me﴾, meaning: and We said to him: Do not associate anything with Me.

His saying: ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate﴾, meaning: those who circumambulate the House.

His saying: ﴿and those who stand [in prayer]﴾, meaning: those who reside [there]. ﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾, meaning: those who pray.

His saying: ﴿And purify My House﴾, meaning: build My House pure.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 27:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And proclaim to mankind the pilgrimage﴾. Ibn Abi Ishaq read "bil-ḥajji" (بِالْحَجِّ) with a kasra on the ḥa' (ḥājj, i.e., the ḥā' is pronounced with a kasra), and likewise throughout the Qur'an. In the narrative: Ibrahim (ʿalayhi al-salam) ascended the Maqam, and the Maqam rose until it became like the tallest mountain in the world. In another narration: he ascended Abu Qubays and then called out: "O people, indeed God, the Exalted, has prescribed the Hajj upon you, so respond to your Lord." Everyone who would perform Hajj answered him, from the wombs of mothers and the loins of fathers. Ibn ʿAbbas said: The first to answer him were the people of Yemen, and they are the most numerous of people in Hajj. So people come saying: "Labbayka Allahumma labbayk" (Here I am, O God, here I am), and this is the response to Ibrahim. It is also narrated that when God, the Exalted, commanded Ibrahim (may the blessings of God be upon him) to call out to the people, he said: "O Lord, how will my voice reach them?" He said: "Upon you is the call, and upon Me is the conveyance."

And His words: ﴿They will come to you on foot﴾, that is: rijalah, meaning those who walk on foot. In some reports: Adam (may the blessings of God be upon him) performed Hajj forty times on foot.

And His words: ﴿and on every lean camel﴾, that is: and upon every lean camel. The ḍāmir (lean one) is the emaciated. Ibn ʿAbbas said: I do not regret anything as much as my regret that I did not perform Hajj on foot, because God, the Exalted, placed those on foot before those who ride.

And His words: ﴿they will come from every deep mountain pass﴾, that is: from every distant path.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 28:

And His saying: ﴿That they may witness benefits for themselves﴾. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali said: "They are forgiveness." Others said: "Benefits for them" means trade. The first opinion is better. It is also said: "The benefits of this world and the Hereafter."

And His saying: ﴿And mention the name of Allah over them on known days﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The known days are the ten (days)." 'Ali and Ibn 'Umar said: "They are the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) and the three days after it."

And His saying: ﴿Over what He has provided for them of the beast of cattle﴾, meaning: when they slaughter them.

And His saying: ﴿So eat from them﴾. This is a command of permission (amr ibahah), not a command of obligation (amr ijab). Some of them said: it is a command of recommendation (amr nadb), and it is recommended to eat from them.

And His saying: ﴿And feed the distressed poor person﴾. The "distressed" (al-ba'is) is the one whose misery has intensified, and "misery" (al-bu's) is destitution. It was also said: the "ba'is" is the one who has been touched by hardship in his time. The meaning of "poor" (al-faqir) is well known.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 30:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That, and whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah﴾. Mujahid said: "The sacred rites of Allah are the Hajj and the 'Umrah." 'Ata' said: "The sacred rites of Allah are what He has forbidden, and a sacred rite (hurmah) is everything that one is forbidden to violate." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "The sacred rites of Allah here are five: the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram), the Sacred City (al-Balad al-Haram), the Sacred Month (al-Shahr al-Haram), the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), and the state of ihram." Some of them said: "Honouring the sacred rites of Allah means that one performs acts of obedience, enjoins them, abandons disobedience, and forbids it."

His saying: ﴿then it is better for him with his Lord﴾. Its meaning: honouring the sacred rites is better for him with Allah in the Hereafter.

His saying: ﴿And the grazing livestock has been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you﴾. "What is recited to you" is the saying of Allah, may He be exalted, in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine﴾, to the end of the verse.

His saying: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾. The "min" here is for specification (li-al-tajnis). Its meaning: avoid the idols, which are an abomination. It is said that rijs and rijz both mean punishment, and the meaning of His saying ﴿So avoid the abomination﴾ is: avoid the cause of punishment.

His saying: ﴿And avoid the word of falsehood﴾, that is, lying. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "I swear, false testimony has been made equal to associating partners with Allah," and he recited this verse: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols and avoid the word of falsehood﴾.

This wording has also been narrated as a marfu' report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

There is another view regarding the verse: that the word of falsehood is shirk. A third view: that the word of falsehood is their talbiyah: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am; You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You, You own him and what he owns."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 31:

And His saying: ﴿Upright before God, not associating anything with Him﴾. The people of tafsir said: The Quraysh used to say: "Whoever performs the hajj, enters the state of ihtinaf (abstaining from what is contrary to the religion) and sacrifices, is a ḥanīf." So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Upright before God, not associating anything with Him﴾, meaning that the ḥanīfiyyah (the state of true monotheism) is only completed by abandoning shirk, and whoever associates partners with God is not a ḥanīf. We have already explained the meaning of ḥanīf earlier.

And His saying: ﴿And whoever associates partners with God, it is as if he had fallen from the sky﴾, i.e., he has fallen from the sky. In some reports from one of the Companions it is related that he said: "I pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God that I would not fall (akhirra) except as a Muslim," i.e., that I would not fall dead except as a Muslim.

And His saying: ﴿Then the birds snatch him away﴾, i.e., the birds seize him and carry him off.

And His saying: ﴿Or the wind throws him into a distant place﴾. i.e., the wind casts him down into a far-off place. The meaning of the verse is that whoever associates partners with God has perished, and has strayed so far from the truth that he can never reach it, for as long as he remains a polytheist.

**Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 32:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is so. And whoever honors the sacred symbols of Allah﴾. Regarding the *sha'ā'ir* (sacred symbols or rites of Allah), there are two opinions. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the *budn* (the sacrificial camels), and honoring them means fattening them and choosing good ones. It is narrated from 'Ata' that the sacred symbols of Allah are the *jimar* (the stoning pillars). And [Zayd] ibn Aslam said: the sacred symbols of Allah are al-Safa and al-Marwah, the Corner (of the Ka'bah), the House, 'Arafah, al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and the *jimar*. Some of them said: the sacred symbols of Allah are the markers of His religion.

His saying: ﴿for indeed it is from the piety of the hearts﴾, that is, this act, and it is, the glorifying (of these symbols), from the piety of the hearts.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 22, verse 33:

And His saying: ﴿For you therein are benefits﴾. ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: it means the benefits of the animal before slaughter, namely riding it, drinking its milk, and other such things. Mujahid said: the benefits in it are before it is designated as an offering (hady); but once it has been designated as an offering, no benefit is to be derived from it. This is also the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and a group of the Companions. The first view was chosen by al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him. Those who hold the first view cite as evidence what has been related: that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw a man driving a camel (badana), and asked him about it, and he said: "It is a badana." So he said: "Ride it, woe to you."

And His saying: ﴿up to an appointed term﴾. According to the first view, the appointed term is the slaughter. According to the second view, the appointed term is the moment of its being designated as a badana. As for if we take the rites (shaʿa'ir) to refer to things other than the camels, then His saying: ﴿For you therein [are benefits]﴾ refers to the reward that Allah the Exalted mentioned for exalting the rites we have mentioned.

And His saying: ﴿then its place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾. The place of sacrifice (mahill) here refers to the time of slaughter and its place.

And His saying: ﴿at the Ancient House﴾. We have already explained it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 34:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And for every community We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: a festival (ʿid). Others said: a place of sacrifice (madhbah). It is also said: a place of worship (mut'abbad).

And His words: ﴿that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them of the beast of cattle﴾. That is: that they may mention the name of Allah Most High over the slaughtering (nahr) of what Allah has provided for them of the beast of cattle.

And His words: ﴿so your God is one God﴾. That is: pronounce the name of Allah Most High alone over the sacrificed animals, for your God is one God.

And His words: ﴿so to Him submit (aslimu)﴾. That is: so to Him devote yourselves sincerely (akhlasu).

And His words: ﴿and give good tidings to the humble (mukhbitin)﴾. Regarding this there are several opinions. The first: it means the humble (mutawadiʿin). Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: it means the sincere (mukhlisin). Others said: it means the righteous (salihin). It is also said: it means the submitting (muslimin). It is reported from 'Amr ibn Aws that he said: they are those who do not wrong, and when they are wronged, they do not seek retribution. Al-Kalbi mentioned that the mukhbitin are those whose hearts are tender. The khabt is the low-lying ground of the earth. Imru' al-Qays said in verse:

(So when we passed the courtyard of the tribe and it turned aside with us into the lowland of Khabt, Dhu Khifaf, the sandy hillock)

And His saying: ﴿Those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾, meaning: their hearts fear.

And His saying: ﴿And the patient ones over what afflicts them﴾, meaning: and give good news to the patient ones over what afflicts them.

And His saying: ﴿And those who establish the prayer﴾, meaning: those who establish the prayer (iqamat al-salah).

And His saying: ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾, its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the camels—We have made them for you among the symbols of Allah﴾. Al-budn is the plural of al-badanah, and it was called badanah for its bulkiness. The camel and the cow are both called badanah, but sheep are not called badanah.

As for His saying ﴿We have made them for you among the symbols of Allah﴾, we have already explained it. Its meaning is: among the markers (a'lam) of the religion of Allah. The budn were called shaʿa'ir (symbols) because they are marked (tushʿar), and marking them is to stab their humps, as is well known in jurisprudence (fiqh). It is reported in the narrations that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, performed his last pilgrimage in his last year. He was throwing the pebble at Jamrat al-ʿAqabah, and a pebble struck his bald head so that blood flowed from it. A man said: "The Commander of the Believers has been marked." When he returned to Madinah, he was killed.

His saying ﴿For you in them is good﴾ we have already explained.

His saying ﴿So mention the name of Allah over them, standing in rows﴾. It is reported from Ibn Masʿud that he recited ṣawāfī (ﷺ), and it is reported from al-Ḥasan al-Basrī that he recited ṣawāfin. The well-known reading is ﴿ṣawāff﴾, and its meaning is lined up in rows (muṣṭaffah). As for ṣawāfī, its meaning is pure (khāliṣah). As for ṣawāfin, it means that the camel is made to stand on three legs, with its left foreleg tied up; this is the ṣufūn. The poet said:

(It has become accustomed to ṣufūn, so that it does not cease to be as if it is a broken one among those that stand on three legs.)

His saying ﴿So when their flanks fall (wajabat junūbuhā)﴾ means: when they fall on their sides.

His saying ﴿So eat from them﴾ we have already explained.

His saying ﴿And feed the contented and the beggar﴾. The well-known view is that al-qāniʿ is the one who asks, and al-muʿtarr is the one who presents himself and does not ask. Mālik said: the best thing I have heard on this is that al-qāniʿ is the muʿtarr, and al-muʿtarr is the one who sees (al-rāʾī). The poet said:

(For those who have much is the right of whoever comes to them, and for those with little is generosity and giving.)

It is also said: al-qāniʿ is the one who is content with what he is given. The well-known view is the first, that al-qāniʿ is the one who asks. It is also said: al-miskīn al-ṭawwāf (the poor man who goes around).

His saying ﴿Thus We have subjected them to you﴾ means: We have made them submissive to you.

His saying ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾: its meaning is apparent.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches Allah﴾. It is related that the polytheists, when they slaughtered, would sprinkle the blood around the House (the Ka'bah), and the Muslims wished to do the same, so Allah the Exalted sent down His saying: ﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches Allah, but it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾. Its meaning: neither the blood nor the flesh reaches Allah the Exalted; rather, piety reaches Him. It has also been said: the blood and flesh do not reach Him except with piety, and it is said: He is not pleased except with piety.

His saying: ﴿Thus He has subjected them to you﴾, meaning: We have made them submissive to you.

His saying: ﴿that you may magnify Allah for having guided you﴾, meaning: that you may exalt Allah for having guided you.

His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to the doers of good﴾. We have already explained the meaning of "the doers of good" earlier.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 22, verse 38:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed.﴾ It is also read: "yadfa'" (He repels). The defending (al-mudafa'ah) of them is by protecting them and giving them victory. It is said: He repels the disbelievers from those who have believed. It is also said: He repels from the believers the whisperings of Satan (wasawis al-shaytan) and the stirrings of the souls (hawajis al-nufus). It is also said: He defends the ignorant through the scholars, and the disobedient through the obedient.

And His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ingrate.﴾ Al-Khawwan is one who is greatly given to betrayal (al-khiyanah), and al-Kafur is one who denies the blessing (kafara al-ni'mah).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 39:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾. The people of tafsir said: this is the first verse revealed concerning the permission to fight. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also recited as "Udhina lil-ladhina yuqatiluna" (أُذِنَ لِلَّذِينَ يُقَاتَلُونَ), with the alif and the ta' vowelled differently, and the reason the verb is cited as "udhina" and "adhina" with both the raised and the accusative vowelling is that the Muslims, before the Hijrah, had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to fight the disbelievers, but he did not grant them permission. When they emigrated to Madinah, Allah the Most High revealed the verses on fighting.

﴿Because they have been wronged﴾, meaning: because they were wronged.

And His words: ﴿And indeed Allah is able to give them victory﴾, meaning: He is capable (qadir).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 40:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who have been expelled from their homes without right﴾, meaning: unjustly.

And His saying: ﴿except that they say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾. Sibawayh said: This is an exceptive that is discontinuous (istithna' munqati'), and its meaning is: "but they were expelled," because they said, "Our Lord is Allah." And some of them said: "but they were expelled" for their monotheism (tawhid).

And His saying: ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others﴾. The well-known view is that the repelling here is the repelling of the mujahidun from the religion and from all the Muslims. And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: [it is the repelling] of those who do not pray by means of those who pray, of those who do not wage jihad by means of the mujahid, and of those who do not know by means of those who know.

And it is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: This is the repelling of the Followers (al-tabi'un) by means of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah. And some of them said: It is the repelling of rights by means of witnesses. And from Qutrub, whose name is Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, who said: It is the repelling of lives by means of retaliation (qisas).

And His saying: ﴿certainly would have been demolished: monasteries and churches﴾, meaning: the monasteries of the monks and the churches of the Christians, ﴿and synagogues﴾ of the Jews, meaning: the places of their prayer. It is also read "wa-Salawat" with a raised sad and lam, the reading of 'Asim al-Jahdari; and it is narrated from al-Dahhak that he read "wa-Suluwat."

And His saying: ﴿and mosques﴾, meaning: the mosques of the believers. Some of them said: the monasteries are for the Christians, the churches for the Jews, and the synagogues (salawat) are the mosques on the roads for the believing travellers, while the mosques (masajid) are the mosques in the cities.

Some of them said: the monasteries are for the Sabians, the churches for the Christians, and the synagogues for the Jews. If someone says: "These places belonging to the disbelievers ought to be demolished, so how does He say, 'would have been demolished'?" The answer to this is that the meaning of the verse is: were it not for Allah's repelling, these places would have been demolished in the time of every prophet. So the monasteries were demolished in the time of Musa, the churches in the time of 'Isa, the synagogues in the time of Dawud and others, and the mosques in the time of Muhammad.

His saying: ﴿in which the name of Allah is much mentioned﴾ has a known meaning.

His saying: ﴿Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Exalted in Might﴾ has an apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 41:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who, if We establish them firmly in the land﴾. This verse relates back to His saying: ﴿And Allah will surely help those who help Him﴾.

And His saying: ﴿They establish prayer, and give zakat, and enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ — the verse was revealed concerning this community. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the verse was revealed concerning the freed captives (tulaqa') of the Banu Hashim. This is a strange (gharib) opinion.

And His saying: ﴿And with Allah rests the outcome of all matters﴾, meaning: the final outcomes (‘awaqib) of matters.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verses 42–44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah denied before them﴾. God, may He be exalted, revealed this verse to console the Prophet and to comfort him. It is as if He said: If your people deny you, ﴿then the people of Noah denied before them, and ʿĀd, and Thamūd, and the people of Ibrahim, and the people of Lut, and the companions of Madyan, and Mūsā was denied﴾. That is, these prophets were denied too.

And His saying: ﴿Then I gave respite to the disbelievers﴾. That is, I granted them a delay, and respite from God is istidraj (gradual enticement toward ruin) and makr (cunning deception).

And His saying: ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My rejection?﴾ That is, My disapproval (nakīr), and His disapproval was by punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verses 42–44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah denied before them﴾. God, may He be exalted, revealed this verse to console the Prophet and to comfort him. It is as if He said: If your people deny you, ﴿then the people of Noah denied before them, and ʿĀd, and Thamūd, and the people of Ibrahim, and the people of Lut, and the companions of Madyan, and Mūsā was denied﴾. That is, these prophets were denied too.

And His saying: ﴿Then I gave respite to the disbelievers﴾. That is, I granted them a delay, and respite from God is istidraj (gradual enticement toward ruin) and makr (cunning deception).

And His saying: ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My rejection?﴾ That is, My disapproval (nakīr), and His disapproval was by punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verses 42–44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they deny you, then the people of Noah denied before them﴾. God, may He be exalted, revealed this verse to console the Prophet and to comfort him. It is as if He said: If your people deny you, ﴿then the people of Noah denied before them, and ʿĀd, and Thamūd, and the people of Ibrahim, and the people of Lut, and the companions of Madyan, and Mūsā was denied﴾. That is, these prophets were denied too.

And His saying: ﴿Then I gave respite to the disbelievers﴾. That is, I granted them a delay, and respite from God is istidraj (gradual enticement toward ruin) and makr (cunning deception).

And His saying: ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My rejection?﴾ That is, My disapproval (nakīr), and His disapproval was by punishment.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 45:

His saying: ﴿So how many a town did We destroy while it was wrongdoing﴾, i.e., how many a town did We destroy.

And His saying: ﴿while it was wrongdoing﴾, i.e., its people were wrongdoers.

And His saying: ﴿so it lies fallen upon its roofs﴾, i.e., collapsed upon its ceilings. Al-khawiyah (fallen, empty) in the language means "the empty." The mention of khawiyah here is because when dwellings collapse, they become empty of their people.

And His saying: ﴿and a well left idle, and a lofty palace﴾. And His saying: ﴿and a lofty palace﴾, i.e., how many a lofty palace whose people have gone and perished. Regarding al-mashid (lofty) there are two opinions: one is that al-mashid is the elevated (al-mutawwal), and the other is that al-mashid is that which is built with shid, and shid is plaster (al-jiss). The poet said:

(He built it with marble and coated it with lime, so for the birds there are nests and lairs in its heights.)

Some of them said: the idle well and the lofty palace were in Yemen; the palace was on the summit of a mountain and the well at its foot. Each of them had a people in great blessing, but they disbelieved, so Allah the Exalted destroyed them, and the well and the palace remained empty of all of them. It is related that Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both, whenever he passed by a ruin, would say: "O ruin, where have your people gone?"

It is related from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said in his sermon: "Where are those who built the cities and raised them? And where are those who built the palaces and plastered them? And where are those who gathered wealth?" Then he recited: ﴿Do you perceive any of them, or hear from them a whisper?﴾

If someone says: What is the benefit of mentioning the idle well and the lofty palace, when there is much of this in the world, so that mentioning this would be of no benefit? The answer to this: it has been the custom of the Arabs to mention abodes for the sake of taking admonition, and they have mentioned such things much in their poetry. Likewise here, Allah the Exalted mentioned the empty palaces and the idle abodes, so that those who take admonition may be admonished thereby.

Al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

(What shall I hope for after the family of Muharriq, who left their dwellings, and after Iyad,)
(the people of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sarir and Barig, and the lofty palace of Sadad,)

(they dwelt at Ankara, over which the waters of the Euphrates flow, coming from the mountains,)
(and I see that bliss, and everything with which one is amused, one day turns to decay and annihilation.)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 46:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land, so that they might have hearts by which they understand?﴾ That is: by which they know. It is said: the intellect (ʿaql) is an innate knowledge (ʿilm gharīzī), and whoever said that its locus is the heart cited this verse as evidence.

His words: ﴿or ears by which they hear?﴾ That is: what is related to them of the reports of the past generations, so that they may take heed from them.

His words: ﴿for indeed it is not the eyes that go blind﴾. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, blindness is blindness of the heart."

Some of them said: there are two eyes in the face and two eyes in the heart. The two eyes in the face are for seeing, and the two eyes in the heart are for taking heed. It is related from Qatadah that he said: the outward sight is for language and benefit, while the sight of the heart is the beneficial sight.

His words: ﴿but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾. Its meaning: the harmful blindness is blindness of the hearts, whereas blindness of the eyes is not harmful in matters of religion. Among what is well known in human speech: "The blind man is not he whose sight has gone, but the blind man is he whose insight has failed."

It is related that Ibn ʿAbbas (raḍiya Allāh ʿanhu) entered upon Muʿawiyah after he had become blind, and his father had become blind at the end of his life, and likewise his grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. Muʿawiyah said to him: "What is the matter with you, O Banu Hashim, that you are afflicted in your eyesight?" Ibn ʿAbbas replied to him: "And what is the matter with you, O Banu Umayyah, that you are afflicted in your insight?"

His words: ﴿the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾ here are by way of emphasis, like the words of the Most High: ﴿they say with their mouths﴾, and like the saying of the speaker: "I saw with my own eyes, and I walked on my own feet."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 47:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will not fail His promise﴾. The verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾, and so on.

And His saying: ﴿but Allah will not fail His promise﴾ means: the promise of punishment.

And His saying: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾ has two interpretations. The first: a day from the days in which Allah created the world is like a thousand years. The second view: its meaning is, a day from the days of their punishment is like a thousand years ﴿of what you count﴾. The second view is the more preferred (al-awla), because the punishment has already been mentioned.

Allah's words: ﴿And how many a town have I given respite while it was wrongdoing﴾ — meaning: I gave it respite.

And His words: ﴿while it was wrongdoing﴾ — meaning: its people were wrongdoers.

And His words: ﴿then I seized it, and to Me is the return﴾ — meaning: the return (al-maṣīr, the place of return).
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "O mankind, I am to you only a clear warner."﴾ That is: a warner, a guide.

And His saying: ﴿So those who have believed and done righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and a generous provision.﴾ The "generous provision" (al-rizq al-karim) is that which never ends, and it is said: it is Paradise.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 51:

As for His saying: ﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to frustrate them﴾, meaning: opposing and hostile (mu'anidin mushaqqin). It has also been read as "mu'jizin" (ـمعجزين), meaning: discouraging people from following the Prophet. It is also said: thinking that they can outdo Us by their claim that there is no resurrection, no Paradise, and no Fire. The meaning of "they outdo Us" is: they escape from Us.

As for His saying: ﴿those are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, meaning: the Fire, and al-Jahim (the Blazing Fire) is an expression for the greatest part of the Fire.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 52:

Concerning the words of the Exalted: ﴿Never did We send before you any messenger or prophet﴾. Ibn 'Abbas recited it as: "nor any muhaddath (one who is inspired)." The Shaykh, the Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Abu 'Ali al-Shafi'i informed us of this, saying: Abu al-Hasan ibn [Firas] informed us, saying: Abu Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid al-Muqri' informed us, from his grandfather Muhammad, from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he recited it in this manner.

So his saying "nor any muhaddath" means: one who is inspired (mulham), as if Allah had spoken to him in his heart. It is well known that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There were muhaddathun (inspired ones) among the nations before you; if there is any among my community, it is 'Umar."

As for the discussion of the messenger (rasul) and the prophet (nabi), some said they are the same. Others distinguished between them, saying: the messenger is the one to whom Jibril (peace be upon him) brings the revelation, while the prophet is the one to whom revelation comes in a dream, or who is inspired by inspiration. Some said: the messenger is one who has a sharia (law) that he preserves, while the prophet is one who was sent to follow the sharia of another and preserves it. They also said: every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger.

Concerning His saying: ﴿except when he desires﴾. Most of them held that its meaning is: when he recites, ﴿Satan throws into his recitation (umniyyatihi)﴾, that is, into his recitation. The poet said about 'Uthman:

(He recited the Book of Allah on the first night, and on its last he met the fate of the decreed death.)

That is, he recited. Some said: "tamanna" is the soul's inner thought. The story behind the verse is what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri, al-Dahhak, and others: that the Prophet recited Surah "al-Najm" in his prayer, while the Muslims and the polytheists were present. It is also said that he recited it during the prayer. When he reached the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾, Satan threw upon his tongue: "Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is indeed to be hoped for." He continued through the surah until he prostrated at its end. The polytheists rejoiced and were delighted, and they said: "He has mentioned our gods with good, and we want nothing but this," and they prostrated along with him.

Ibn Mas'ud said: Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira did not prostrate; he raised some dust to his forehead and said: "I have prostrated," for he was an elderly man. He said: Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came and said: "Recite to me Surah al-Najm." He recited it, and Satan cast upon his tongue this (phrase) as well. Jibril said: "I did not bring this," and he removed it from his recitation. The Messenger of Allah became deeply grieved, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse to him: ﴿Never did We send before you any messenger or prophet, except that when he desired, Satan threw into his desire﴾.

If someone says: How is this permissible for the Prophet, when he was protected from error in the foundations of the religion? Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, over My servants you have no authority﴾, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾, meaning Iblis?

The answer to this: they differed in answering it. Some said: this was cast by some hypocrites into his recitation; the hypocrite was the reader, so the polytheists thought the Messenger had recited it, and that hypocrite was called a devil (shaytan), because every rebellious disbeliever stands in the position of a devil. This answer is weak.

Others said: the Messenger did not recite it, but Satan uttered this in the midst of the Prophet's recitation, and the polytheists heard it and thought the Messenger had recited it. This is the view chosen by al-Azhari and others.

Some said: the Messenger dozed off briefly and drowsed, so this came upon his tongue, and he had no knowledge of Satan's casting. This is the view of Qatada. As for most of the early scholars (salaf), they held that this was something that passed over the Messenger's tongue through Satan's casting, without his believing in it. That was a trial and a test from Allah, and Allah tests His servants with whatever He wills and afflicts them with whatever He desires, and no one has any objection against Him. They said: although this was a grave error, error is permissible for the prophets, except that they are not left to persist in it.

It is also reported from some that a devil called al-Abyad (the White) did this, and in some narrations it is said that he appeared in the form of Jibril and inserted this into his recitation. And Allah knows best.

Concerning His saying: ﴿then Allah abrogates what Satan casts﴾, meaning: Allah removes what Satan casts.

Concerning His saying: ﴿then Allah firmly establishes His verses﴾, meaning: Allah makes His verses firm.

Concerning His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knowing, Wise﴾, its meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, i.e., a test and a calamity.

And His saying: ﴿And the hard of heart﴾, i.e., those whose hearts are stiff against accepting the truth.

And His saying: ﴿And indeed the wrongdoers are in extreme dissension﴾, i.e., in a long-lasting opposition. It was also said: "constant," and this is the better view.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 54:

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And that those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord﴾, means: [that it is] what He has affirmed and not abrogated (naskh).

And His statement: ﴿so that they believe in it﴾ (i.e., they hold it as true, from Allah, Exalted is He).

And His statement: ﴿and their hearts humble themselves to it﴾, i.e., their hearts become tranquil in it.

And His statement: ﴿And indeed, Allah is the Guide of those who have believed to a straight path﴾, i.e., to an upright way, which is Islam.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 55:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt concerning it﴾, i.e., in doubt about it.

And His saying: ﴿until the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾. It was said: it is death; and it was said: it is the Resurrection.

And His saying: ﴿or there comes to them the punishment of a barren day﴾. In this there are two views. The first: that the barren day is the Day of Resurrection. The second view: that the barren day is the Day of Badr, and this is the view of most scholars. It is related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: "Four verses concern the Day of Badr. The first is His saying: ﴿the punishment of a barren day﴾. The second is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the day when We will seize with the greatest seizure﴾. The third is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So it will be inevitable﴾. The fourth is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We will surely make them taste a punishment nearer than the greater punishment﴾." So the killing on the Day of Badr is the nearer punishment. As for "barren" (ʿaqīm) in the language, it means prevention. It is said: a man is ʿaqīm and a woman is ʿaqīm when they are prevented from having children; and a wind is ʿaqīm when it brings no rain; and a day is ʿaqīm when there is in it no good and no blessing. (So the Day of Badr is a barren day, because there was in it no good and no blessing) for the disbelievers.

The poet said:
(The women have become barren, so they bear none like him... Indeed the women, with one like him, are barren.)

The Most High's saying: ﴿The Dominion that Day belongs to Allah; He will judge between them﴾ means: He will decide between them.

And His saying: ﴿So those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in Gardens of Bliss﴾ is clear in its meaning.
And His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ — i.e., one that degrades and disgraces.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 58:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who emigrated in the way of Allah and then were killed or died, Allah will surely provide for them a good provision.﴾ The good provision (al-rizq al-hasan) is that which never ends, and that is the provision of Paradise.

And His saying: ﴿And indeed, Allah is the best of providers.﴾ That is, the most excellent of providers.

Verse 22:59 says: ﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance which they will be pleased with﴾. It is also read "mudkhalan" with a fatha on the meem, and "al-mudkhal" with a damma is from the verb of causing entry (al-idkhal), while "al-mudkhal" with a fatha means the place.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Forbearing﴾, meaning: Knowing of the deeds of the servants, Forbearing toward them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 22, verse 60:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is so. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾. It is related that a people among the Muslims encountered a people among the polytheists at the end of al-Muharram, and two nights of it remained. The polytheists barred the Muslims, so the Muslims said to them: "Desist, for this is a sacred month." But they did not desist, so the Muslims fought them in self-defence, and they prevailed. Then God, exalted is He, sent down this verse.

It is also said: a people among the polytheists killed a people among the Muslims, so the Prophet (ﷺ) overcame them and killed them, and God, exalted is He, sent down this verse. The first act was called a "punishment" (ʿuqūba), although in reality the term ʿuqūba applies to what is a recompense for a crime, but this is due to the balance of the speech (izdiwāj al-kalām), since it was mentioned in correspondence with the punishment. This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then he is wronged by him﴾, al-baghy (wrongdoing/oppression) here refers to what the polytheists did to the Muslims of injustice, expulsion from their homes, and seizure of their wealth.

As for His saying: ﴿Surely God will assist him﴾, its meaning is apparent.

As for His saying: ﴿Surely God is Pardoning, Forgiving﴾, i.e., He is one who overlooks and pardons the Muslims.
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because God causes the night to enter into the day﴾ ... the verse. The meaning is apparent.

This is a commentary on Qur'an 22:62 by al-Sam'ani.

"That is because Allah, He is the Truth" (dhalika bi-anna Allaha huwa al-haqq): meaning, He is the Possessor of truth (dhu al-haqq).

"And that what they call upon besides Him is the falsehood" (wa-anna ma yad'una min dunihi huwa al-batil): meaning, it is not true (laysa bi-haqq).

"And that Allah, He is the Most High, the Great" (wa-anna Allaha huwa al-'Ali al-Kabir): meaning, the One who is exalted and magnified. It is said that al-'Ali here refers to the religion, meaning: His religion rises above the (other) religions. Al-Kabir is one of His attributes, blessed and exalted is He.
